newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr climb struggles with gravity.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr climb struggles with gravity.

text.p: The Australian dollar nudged higher Monday to probe resistance-laden space above 79 cents, but lacked the momentum to escape long standing ranges.

Asian funds were light buyers through the day and corporate bids were providing a solid base around US$0.7880 on which the currency could slowly extend its two-week one-cent rally. There was the usual talk of samurai demand, but dealers doubted the pace of issues would be enough to overtake US$/yen weakness.
"There's nothing to get the market going," said one dealer, echoing a well worn lament. "People are even using terms like "natural level" for the AUD, and that's just not natural."
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had topped out at US$0.7910/15 after orbiting US$0.7910 all session.
It ended Friday at US$0.7904/09 having crept from US$0.7860 earlier in the week and a US$0.7815 low the week before, both of which were now key support levels.
Months of indecisive trading between 78 and 80 cents had also left the ground ahead littered with resistance levels with US$0.7925, US$0.7945 and US$0.7985 some of the most meaningful.
On the crosses, the currency drifted to 87.87/97 yen from 88.06/16 late Friday as it closely tracked a jittery US$/yen and in trade weighted terms was unchanged through the day at 58.1.
The U.S. currency was stuck near 111.00 yen having slumped from atop 114.00 in the last fortnight as the market scented a shift in Japanese policy against a weaker yen.

Both dollars won a surprise boost this morning when Japan reported its trade surplus had fallen 13 percent to 470.9 billion yen in October against market expectations of the first year-on-year rise in 23 months.
But the data were not entirely favourable since Japan's surplus with the U.S. -- the problem that had so exercised politicians and markets in the past -- leapt 31 percent to 354.8 billion.
There was little on the domestic front to excite this week the ground this week with the only major data being merchandise imports on Tuesday and company profits on Thursday.
Imports are seen rising a marginal 0.5 percent matching the gain made in September, although estimates range from a 2.0 percent fall to a 4.0 percent rise.

Analysts will be focused on the performance of capital imports which have slowed in recent months raising concerns business investment might not live up to the high expectations of the government abnd the Reserve Bank. Another weak capital imports figure, therefore, could bruise dollar sentiment.
Company profits are expected to be flat in the September quarter after a 1.4 percent fall in Q2.
Analysts caution this somewhat arcane survey series is hard to forecast with any measure of confidence and estimates ranged from a fall of 3.0 percent to a rise of 2.5 percent.

Since these, along with the seperately reported profits of smaller companies, feed into the income-measure of GDP a result at the edge of expectations would imply a substantial revision to GDP expectations was needed.
